intro: If you are a solo lawyer without an AI policy, you are in the majority. Clio's 2026 report, as summarized by the NC Bar, finds 57% of solo practitioners have no AI policy, even though 71% use AI. The risk is not the tool itself. It is the lack of written rules about what goes in, what gets checked, and who signs off.
tldr: Most solos use AI, and most have no written policy. That gap is the problem.
ABA Formal Opinion 512 says managerial lawyers must set clear firm rules on generative AI use.
Client information needs informed consent before it goes into self-learning tools.

blocks.text: What a solo lawyer without an AI policy risks today

The short version is this. A solo practice with no AI policy has no written answer to three questions. Which tools may you use? Which client facts may go into them? Who checks the output before it reaches a court or a client? Most solos never answer these in writing. They answer them in practice, one email at a time.

The numbers back this up. The NC Bar's summary of Clio's 2026 report says 57% of solo practitioners have no AI policy, and 55% of small firms have none. Yet 71% of solos and 75% of small firms use AI. You are not behind on the tools. You may be behind on the paperwork.

The 8am 2026 Legal Industry Report, which covered more than 1,300 legal professionals, asked a wider question. Only 9% of respondents say their firm has a written policy that is enforced. Those figures cover firms of every size, so read them as a broad signal, not a solo-only count.

blocks.caption: Clio 2026 figures, as reported by the NC Bar. Clio's own pages were not available to check.

blocks.text: How a missing policy turns into an error

Take a solo who drafts a demand letter on a Friday afternoon. They ask an AI tool for supporting cases, paste in a few client facts to get the wording right, and send the letter on Monday. Nothing in that sequence looks unusual. Each step lacks a rule, so nobody stops it. A policy closes exactly that gap.
Walk through your own last matter and mark each point where an AI tool touched the work. Most people find more of these points than they expected.

items: The research step: an AI answer names a case you never opened.
The input step: client names and facts go into a tool with no consent on file.
The drafting step: a generated quote or citation goes into the letter unchanged.
The filing step: no second reader checks the citations before they leave your desk.

blocks.text: The Charlotin database is a useful map of where this goes wrong. It counts warnings as well as sanctions, so do not treat its total as a fine count. Read a few entries yourself. Note which step from the list above each one skipped.

Research tools carry their own risk. Test yours before you trust it. Ask a question where you already know the answer, then check whether every citation exists and says what the tool claims. Repeat the test every few months and write the result in your policy file.
Why solo and small firms skip the policy
Most solos do not ignore the question. They run out of time for it. The causes below are the ones the sources point to. Start with the one that is specific to a practice of one.
You are the manager and the supervisor

ABA Formal Opinion 512 separates two roles. Managerial lawyers must set clear policies on the firm's permissible use of generative AI. Supervisory lawyers must make reasonable efforts to make sure the firm's lawyers and nonlawyers comply. In a larger firm, different people may hold those roles. In a solo practice, one person holds both. That is why the gap is common and easy to miss.
Time is the first barrier

Clio's 2026 figures, as the NC Bar reports them, name finding time as the biggest barrier to adopting new technology for 27% of solos and 33% of small firms. A policy never feels urgent. It sits behind the brief that is due tomorrow. The fix is to schedule it, not to wait for a free hour.
Fixes you can use today without buying anything

None of these fixes needs a new subscription. You need Pages, which comes with the Mac, and a calendar. If you already pay for Microsoft 365, you can use Word and Outlook too. Each fix below can be done alone, and each one leaves a file you keep.
Write one page in Pages

Open Pages from Applications. Choose File > New, then pick a blank template. Type the title AI use policy and today's date. Under it, add five headings: approved tools, client data, checking output, training, and review date. Write one or two sentences under each. A page you finish beats a long draft you never send.

Keep the wording plain. Say what you allow, not what you fear. For example: 'Use only tools on the approved list. Never enter client names or case facts into a tool that is not approved for client data.' That line gives your future self a clear rule to follow.
Inventory every AI tool you touched this month

Open your recent work and list each tool. Include Word and Outlook features, Chrome extensions, and the Copilot app. Microsoft's support page says you can sign in to Copilot on a Mac with a Microsoft 365 work or school account or a personal Microsoft account. Write down which account you used. A personal account on client work is a blind spot worth checking.

items: The name, and how you open it, such as Copilot with Option + Spacebar.
The account you sign in with, work or personal.
Whether the tool's own terms say it stores what you type.
The kinds of information you used with it this month.

blocks.text: Sort client data into three tiers

Use three tiers. Tier one is public information, such as published statutes. Tier two is your own business information, such as rates and invoices. Tier three is anything about a client or a matter. Approved tools may touch tiers one and two. Tier three goes only into tools you have vetted and cleared with the client, as the next section explains.
Add AI consent to your engagement letter

The NCBE summary of Opinion 512 says informed client consent is required before you input information relating to the representation into self-learning tools. It says boilerplate waivers are not enough. The article calls the engagement agreement a logical place to make that disclosure. Keep the wording specific to the tools you actually use.

A sample sentence to adapt after checking your state bar's rules: 'I may use generative AI tools to help with your matter. Before I enter information about your matter into a tool that learns from its inputs, I will name the tool and ask for your consent.'

blocks.title: Check your rules first
blocks.text: Confidentiality duties apply to every tool you use. Follow your state bar's rules, and your employer's rules if you work in a firm, before you enter any client facts.
Check citations, train yourself, and set a review date

Verification stops most of the errors described above. Open every case and every quote at its original source before it goes into a filing or a client letter. Keep the court's site in one Chrome tab and your draft in another. Lazur can run background research for you, but you still open each source yourself.

Training is the part most people skip. The NCBE article lists what Opinion 512 training should cover: how to use the tools, the ethical issues, protecting confidential client information, and secure data handling and privacy. As a solo, you are both the trainee and the trainer. Write a short checklist with those four topics, and tick each one off when you have tested it.

Set a review date now, before you forget. Open Calendar, press ⌘N, and create a repeating event that comes back every quarter. In the event notes, list the three questions the policy answers: which tools, which client facts, and who checks the output.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen. It answers out loud and points at things. Ask where a setting sits in Word, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.

When you ask how to do something, Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click, and you press the button yourself. It does not click buttons, edit files, or run other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for Word, Outlook, or any other app, and no app maker has partnered with it.

Hold fn to dictate. Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app, which helps when you talk through a draft. Snippets and a personal dictionary can hold the standard phrases you reuse, such as your consent sentence.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. That still may not fit client work. If the screen shows client facts, check your engagement terms and your state bar's rules first.
A one-week plan to get this done

Spread the work across short sessions over one week. Each session ends with a file you can open the next morning. The order matters. The inventory comes first, because every other rule depends on which tools you actually use.
Mistakes people make with a first AI policy

items: Writing a policy nobody reads. Keep it to one page you can read in one sitting.
Banning AI outright. A ban often pushes use onto personal accounts, which is the blind spot the inventory is meant to catch.
Copying a big-firm template without checking your state's rules.
Assuming a free tool keeps client data private. Read that tool's own terms first.
Writing the policy once and never reviewing it.
Skipping consent because a client seems relaxed about technology.

Start with the inventory tonight. Open Pages, press ⌘N, and create a blank page called AI use policy. Then read ABA Formal Opinion 512 and your state bar's guidance, since sources disagree on how strictly the rules apply. For the document side, see the [Word guide for lawyers](/for/lawyers/word). faq.question: Does a solo lawyer need a written AI policy?
faq.answer: The NCBE summary of ABA Formal Opinion 512 says managerial lawyers must establish clear policies on generative AI use. A solo lawyer is both the managing and the supervising lawyer, so the duty lands on you. Sources disagree on how strictly it applies, so read the opinion and your state bar's rules before you rely on this summary.

faq.question: Is a policy enough, or do I need training too?
faq.answer: The NCBE article lists training topics for Opinion 512: how to use the tools, the ethical issues, protecting confidential client information, and secure data handling and privacy. A policy without training is a document nobody follows. Training without a policy has no rules to teach.

faq.question: Can I put client information into a free AI tool?
faq.answer: Under the NCBE summary of Opinion 512, informed client consent is required before you input information relating to the representation into self-learning tools. Boilerplate waivers are not enough. Check the tool's terms too, and confirm your state's rules before you enter any client facts.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my screen to someone?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut, ⌥ ⌘. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. If a screen shows client facts, follow your engagement terms and your state bar's rules first.

faq.question: Is there a free trial?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur has a Pro trial that does not need a credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. Check the pricing page for the current plans and terms before you decide.

faq.question: I work inside a firm. Does this page still apply?
faq.answer: Partly. A firm usually has its own AI rules, and you must follow them. For regulated work such as law, nursing, or accounting, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data, even if a template suggests otherwise. Use this page to ask better questions, not to set firm policy alone.

faq.question: Does Copilot on Mac need a work account?
faq.answer: No. Microsoft's support page says you can sign in to the Copilot app on a Mac with a Microsoft 365 work or school account or a personal Microsoft account. That choice matters for client data, so use the account your firm allows. Option + Spacebar opens the prompt window by default. Copilot Pages and Deep Research are not available on macOS.

costs.title: Errors that reach a court
costs.text: The Charlotin database, last updated 5 November 2026, lists 2,266 AI hallucination cases identified so far. 898 involve a lawyer party, and 1,535 come from US courts. The count includes warnings, not only sanctions. A solo has no second reader to catch a bad citation before it is filed.

costs.title: Wrong answers from research tools
costs.text: A 2024 Stanford study found leading AI legal research tools hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time. Those tests used 2024 products, so current tools may differ. Until your own tests show otherwise, assume any AI-supplied case needs a check against the original source.

costs.title: Client confidentiality and consent
costs.text: The NCBE summary of Opinion 512 says informed client consent is required before you enter information about a matter into a self-learning tool. Boilerplate waivers are not enough. Entering client facts without that consent breaks the rule the summary describes, even when the output looks correct.

costs.title: No training on your own habits
costs.text: 54% of respondents to the 8am 2026 report say their firm provides no training on responsible AI use and has no plans to. In a solo practice, the training gap is you. Nobody else checks whether your prompts include client names or case details.

costs.title: Revenue you do not capture
costs.text: In Thomson Reuters' 2025 survey, organizations with a visible AI strategy were twice as likely as those with informal adoption to see AI-driven revenue growth. Only 22% had one. The survey covered professionals across fields and measured self-reported results. No source found prices this gap for a solo firm.

costs.title: Slower work than you need
costs.text: A 2026 study of AI-powered lawyering reported productivity gains of roughly 50% to 130% in five of six tested legal tasks. Its results are not settled across sources, so treat them as a direction, not a forecast. Without a policy, you cannot safely use AI on the tasks where it helps.

causes.title: You are the manager and the supervisor
causes.text: ABA Formal Opinion 512 names two roles, managerial and supervisory. In a larger firm, different people can share them. In a solo practice, one person has to write the policy and enforce it. Nobody else is assigned the job, so it tends to stay undone.

causes.title: Time beats policy every week
causes.text: Clio's 2026 figures, as the NC Bar reports them, say finding time is the biggest barrier to adopting new technology for 27% of solos and 33% of small firms. A policy has no deadline. Client work always has one, so the policy loses every week until it is scheduled.

causes.title: AI arrives inside tools you already use
causes.text: Copilot, Word, and Chrome now offer AI features without a new purchase. That makes adoption easy and rules hard. Microsoft's support page says Copilot on a Mac can be signed in with a personal account as well as a work account, so the default choice may not match your firm's rules.

causes.title: The rule feels unclear
causes.text: Sources do not agree on how strictly the duty applies. The NCBE article reads Opinion 512 as requiring clear policies, while other sources disagree on whether a written policy is mandatory. Uncertainty tends to produce waiting, and waiting produces no policy.

causes.title: Nobody asks, and few plan one
causes.text: The 8am 2026 report found 43% of respondents say their firm has no formal AI policy and no plans to create one. Without a trigger, a policy stays on the to-do list. The fix is to tie the policy to a date and a task you already do.

fixes.title: Write one page in Pages
fixes.text: Open Pages, choose File > New, and pick a blank template. Title the page AI use policy and add the date. Create five headings: approved tools, client data, checking output, training, and review date. A short page you finish is more useful than a long draft that never leaves your desk.

fixes.title: Inventory every AI tool you touched this month
fixes.text: List each tool, where you open it, the account you signed in with, and the kinds of information you used with it. Check each tool's own terms for storage and training. Anything you cannot classify goes in the no-client-data tier until you know more.

fixes.title: Sort client data into three tiers
fixes.text: Tier one is public information. Tier two is your own business information. Tier three is anything about a client or a matter. Approved tools may touch tiers one and two. Tier three goes only into tools you have vetted and cleared with the client.

fixes.title: Add AI consent to your engagement letter
fixes.text: Add a specific paragraph to your engagement letter that names the tools you use and asks for consent before you enter matter information. The NCBE article calls the engagement agreement a logical place for that disclosure. Have your state bar's rules checked before you send it.

fixes.title: Check every citation at the source
fixes.text: Open each case, statute, and quote at its original source before it goes into a filing or letter. Use a Chrome tab for the court's site and another for your draft. Mark each citation as checked in your draft so nothing slips past you.

fixes.title: Train yourself with a short checklist
fixes.text: Use the four topics the NCBE article lists for Opinion 512 training: how to use the tools, the ethical issues, protecting confidential client information, and secure data handling and privacy. Tick each topic off after you test it on a practice question, not a real matter.

fixes.title: Set a review date in Calendar
fixes.text: Open Calendar, press ⌘N, and create a repeating event for each quarter. Put the three questions your policy answers in the event notes: which tools, which client facts, and who checks the output. A review you schedule is more likely to happen.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Write down every AI tool
plan.text: Open the tools you used last month. Include Word, Outlook, Chrome extensions, and any Copilot sign-in. Note which account each one uses, then save the list as a page in Pages.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Sort your client data
plan.text: Use three tiers: public, your business information, and client information. Mark which tools may touch each tier. If a tool is unclear, it goes in the no-client-data tier.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Draft the one-page policy
plan.text: Open Pages, press ⌘N, and draft the five headings. Ask Lazur to draft a first version, then edit every line yourself. Keep each rule short enough to read aloud.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Add consent and checking rules
plan.text: Write a consent sentence for your engagement letter, and check it against your state bar's rules. Add a rule that every citation gets opened at its original source before it is filed or sent.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Set training and a review date
plan.text: Block a short training session on the four topics from the NCBE summary. Create a repeating Calendar event for the review, then date and save the policy.
